summary: Modern Hebrew has no cases: a noun never changes its ending for its role in the sentence. הַיֶּלֶד “the boy” is the same word as subject, as object and after a preposition — so the “subject form” (nominative) is simply the dictionary form, with nothing to learn. What does the job of the cases instead: (1) word order — normally subject – verb – object, and in a verbless sentence the subject comes first (הַסֵּפֶר פֹּה); (2) the small word אֶת before a definite direct object (lesson 7: הוּא קוֹרֵא אֶת הַסֵּפֶר), which works like a one-word accusative; (3) prepositions, most of them prefixes (lessons 11–13: לַיֶּלֶד “to the boy”, בַּבַּיִת “in the house”, מֵהַבַּיִת “from the house”); (4) agreement: a present-tense verb agrees with its subject in gender and number, which also shows who the subject is. Old Semitic had three case endings (-u, -a, -i), which Arabic still has; Hebrew lost them before the Bible was written. The construct state (בֵּית סֵפֶר “school”, from בַּיִת) is not a case: it changes the first noun of a pair to show that the next noun belongs to it, whatever the role of the pair in the sentence.

head: role
Hebrew (no case)

blocks.caption: The same noun in three roles. Hebrew keeps הַיֶּלֶד unchanged and adds a word or a prefix where needed.

blocks.text: For now, in lessons 1–4, this means: the noun you learn is already the form you use as a subject. זֶה סֵפֶר, הַסֵּפֶר פֹּה, הַסֵּפֶר הָיָה שָׁם — סֵפֶר never changes for its role, only for number (סְפָרִים) and definiteness (הַסֵּפֶר).

blocks.title: What replaces the cases
blocks.text: Word order (subject before the verb), אֶת before a definite direct object, prepositions (mostly the prefixes בְּ, לְ, מִ), and the agreement of the verb with its subject.

blocks.title: Not a case: the construct state
blocks.text: בַּיִת → בֵּית סֵפֶר, דִּירָה → דִּירַת סְטוּדֶנְטִים. The first noun changes shape because another noun follows and “belongs” to it — the change happens in any role, so it is not a case.

blocks.title: Pronouns look like cases, but are prepositions
blocks.text: “me” as an object is אוֹתִי, “to me” is לִי: these are אֶת and לְ with a pronoun suffix (lessons 6–7), not case forms of אֲנִי.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when you translate a case form
questions: Is it the subject? → the plain noun, usually first.
Is it a definite direct object? → אֶת + the noun (lesson 7).
Is it after a preposition? → the Hebrew preposition, usually a prefix, + the plain noun.

askYourself: Which role does the noun have: subject, direct object, or after a preposition?
Subject → the dictionary form, unchanged; put it before the verb (or first in a verbless sentence).
Definite direct object → אֶת before it (from lesson 7); indefinite → nothing.
Other roles → a preposition (בְּ, לְ, מִ, עִם …) before the unchanged noun.
Did I change the noun’s ending for its role? → undo it: Hebrew nouns change only for number, definiteness and the construct state.

traps: Do not look for case endings: הַיֶּלֶד is the same as subject and object.
אֶת is not a preposition meaning “to”: it only marks a definite direct object and is not translated.
The construct state (בֵּית־, דִּירַת־) is not a genitive case of the first noun.
Biblical traces such as the -ָה of לַיְלָה (Wiktionary: probably an old accusative) are fossils, not a living case.

quiz.q: How many case endings does a Modern Hebrew noun have?
quiz.why: הַיֶּלֶד stays הַיֶּלֶד in every role; Arabic has -u / -a / -i, German changes the article (der / den / dem).

quiz.q: What is the Hebrew “subject form” of סֵפֶר?
quiz.why: The subject is the plain noun: סֵפֶר / הַסֵּפֶר. סִפְרוֹ is “his book”, and אֶת marks a definite object.

quiz.q: Which word will mark a definite direct object (lesson 7)?
quiz.why: הוּא קוֹרֵא אֶת הַסֵּפֶר “he reads the book” — אֶת is untranslated; שֶׁל means “of”, עִם “with”.

quiz.q: בַּיִת becomes בֵּית in בֵּית סֵפֶר. Is that a case?
options: no — it is the construct state
quiz.answer: no — it is the construct state
quiz.why: The first noun changes because another noun is attached to it, in any role of the sentence.

quiz.q: What shows the subject in הַמּוֹרֶה פֹּה?
options: its place at the start of the sentence
quiz.answer: its place at the start of the sentence
quiz.why: Word order (and later the agreement of the verb) does the work of the nominative.

quiz.q: Which language of the course still has the old Semitic case endings -u, -a, -i?
quiz.why: Classical / Modern Standard Arabic keeps them (الْوَلَدُ / الْوَلَدَ / الْوَلَدِ); Hebrew lost them before the Biblical period.

seeAlso.note: Arabic keeps three cases on the noun’s ending (-u nominative, -a accusative, -i genitive); Hebrew, its sister, lost them and uses word order, אֶת and prepositions.
German has four cases, shown mostly by the article (der / den / dem / des); Hebrew’s article הַ never changes.
Chinese has no cases either: as in Hebrew, the place in the sentence shows who does what.

notes.text: Greek marks the role on the article and the noun (ο φίλος / τον φίλο / του φίλου); Hebrew keeps הַחָבֵר unchanged and adds אֶת before a definite object, or a preposition.
Russian changes the ending for every role (друг / друга / другу); Hebrew never does — the form you learn is the only form: הַחָבֵר.
As in Spanish, nouns have no cases. Spanish a before a personal object (veo a Juan) and Hebrew אֶת before a definite object are both small words, not endings.

As in English, nouns do not change for their role; word order and small words (אֶת, prepositions) do the work. Even pronoun objects are אֶת or a preposition with an ending (אוֹתִי, לִי), not a separate case.
French nouns have no cases either; the only extra is אֶת, a small word before a definite direct object.
German shows the case on the article (der / den / dem Freund); Hebrew has no cases at all — הַחָבֵר in every role.
Hindi nouns take an oblique form before a postposition (लड़का → लड़के को); Hebrew nouns never change: הַיֶּלֶד, לַיֶּלֶד, עִם הַיֶּלֶד.
Persian nouns have no case endings either; Persian را after a definite object is the mirror image of Hebrew אֶת before it.
Marathi nouns take an oblique stem and case suffixes (मुलगा → मुलाला “to the boy”); Hebrew nouns stay the same and take a preposition.
Arabic keeps three case endings (-u, -a, -i: الْوَلَدُ / الْوَلَدَ / الْوَلَدِ); Hebrew lost them — הַיֶּלֶד is the same in every role.
Turkish marks the role with suffixes (ev, evi, eve, evde, evden); Hebrew has no such suffixes: אֶת before a definite object, and prefixes such as לְ, בְּ, מִ.
Japanese marks roles with particles after the noun (が, を, に); Hebrew uses word order and small words before the noun (אֶת, לְ, בְּ).
Korean role particles follow the noun (이 / 가, 을 / 를); Hebrew uses word order, אֶת and prepositions before the noun.
Finnish has more than a dozen cases; Hebrew has none — prepositions and אֶת do their job.
Hungarian marks roles with case suffixes (-t, -ban, -ból …); Hebrew has none.
Swahili nouns have no case endings either; roles come from word order, the verb prefixes and small words — in Hebrew from word order, אֶת and prepositions.
Luganda nouns have no case endings; roles come from word order and the verb prefixes. Hebrew relies on word order, אֶת and prepositions.
As in Chinese, Hebrew nouns never change for their role; word order and small words (אֶת, prepositions) do the work.
As in Vietnamese, the noun has one form in every role; word order and small words show who does what.
Inuktitut has many cases and ergative alignment (the subject of a transitive verb takes its own ending); Hebrew has no cases and treats every subject alike.
